sql-chinook-invoices-per-country-min-ten.title: Countries with at least ten invoices
sql-chinook-invoices-per-country-min-ten.prompt_md:
Using the **Invoice** table in the Chinook database, count how many invoices were billed to each country and keep only the countries that have **at least 10** invoices.

Return exactly two columns:
- `Country` — the value of `BillingCountry`
- `InvoiceCount` — the number of invoices billed to that country

Sort the result by `InvoiceCount` in **descending** order; break ties by `Country` in **ascending** (A→Z) order.
sql-chinook-invoices-per-country-min-ten.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- BillingCountry AS Country,
  -- COUNT(*) AS InvoiceCount
FROM Invoice
-- GROUP BY ...
-- HAVING ...
-- ORDER BY ...;
hints: Filtering on an aggregate like COUNT(*) requires HAVING, not WHERE.
Add Country as a secondary sort key so rows with equal counts have a fixed order.
sql-chinook-invoices-per-country-min-ten.explanation_md: Group the invoices by `BillingCountry` and use `COUNT(*)` to tally invoices per country. A `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10` clause filters out small countries after aggregation (you cannot use `WHERE` for an aggregate). Finally, sort by the count descending with `Country` as a deterministic tie-breaker.

sql-chinook-top-genres-by-revenue.title: Top five genres by revenue
sql-chinook-top-genres-by-revenue.prompt_md:
Find the five genres that generated the most revenue in the Chinook store. Line-level revenue is `InvoiceLine.UnitPrice * InvoiceLine.Quantity`. Join **InvoiceLine** → **Track** → **Genre** to attribute each sold line to a genre.

Return exactly two columns:
- `Genre` — the genre name (`Genre.Name`)
- `Revenue` — the total revenue for that genre, rounded to **2 decimal places**

Sort by `Revenue` in **descending** order; break ties by `Genre` ascending. Return only the **top 5** rows.
sql-chinook-top-genres-by-revenue.starter_code:
SELECT g.Name AS Genre,
       ROUND(SUM(il.UnitPrice * il.Quantity), 2) AS Revenue
FROM InvoiceLine il
-- JOIN Track ...
-- JOIN Genre ...
-- GROUP BY ...
-- ORDER BY ...
-- LIMIT 5;
hints: Each sold line's revenue is UnitPrice * Quantity from InvoiceLine.
You need two joins to get from InvoiceLine to a genre name.
sql-chinook-top-genres-by-revenue.explanation_md: Revenue lives on `InvoiceLine`, but the genre lives on `Track`/`Genre`, so two joins connect the sale to its genre. Summing `UnitPrice * Quantity` per genre gives revenue; `ROUND(..., 2)` keeps currency tidy, and `LIMIT 5` after the descending sort returns the leaders.

sql-chinook-tracks-per-media-type.title: Track count per media type
sql-chinook-tracks-per-media-type.prompt_md:
Count how many tracks exist for each media type in the Chinook catalog by joining **Track** to **MediaType**.

Return exactly two columns:
- `MediaType` — the media type name (`MediaType.Name`)
- `TrackCount` — the number of tracks of that media type

Sort by `TrackCount` in **descending** order; break ties by `MediaType` ascending.
sql-chinook-tracks-per-media-type.starter_code:
SELECT m.Name AS MediaType,
       COUNT(*) AS TrackCount
FROM Track t
-- JOIN MediaType ...
-- GROUP BY ...
-- ORDER BY ...;
hints: Group by the media type's Name and count rows in Track.
MediaTypeId links Track to MediaType.
sql-chinook-tracks-per-media-type.explanation_md: Join `Track` to `MediaType` on `MediaTypeId`, group by the media type name, and use `COUNT(*)` to tally tracks. Ordering by the count descending (with the name as a tie-breaker) surfaces the most common formats first.

sql-chinook-tracks-priced-above-one-doll.title: Premium-priced tracks
sql-chinook-tracks-priced-above-one-doll.prompt_md:
Using the **Track** table in the Chinook database, the merchandising team wants to review every track that is priced above the standard $0.99 tier. Return the tracks whose `UnitPrice` is strictly greater than `0.99`.

Output exactly two columns named `Name` and `UnitPrice`. Sort the result by `UnitPrice` descending, then by `Name` ascending (A to Z) to break ties.
sql-chinook-tracks-priced-above-one-doll.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- your columns here
FROM Track
-- add your filter and sort
;
hints: Use a single comparison in the WHERE clause; strictly greater than means `>`, not `>=`.
When two rows share the same price, the secondary sort key (Name ascending) decides their order.
sql-chinook-tracks-priced-above-one-doll.explanation_md: Filter rows with a simple `WHERE UnitPrice > 0.99` comparison, then apply a two-key `ORDER BY` so ties on price are broken alphabetically by name. No joins or aggregation are needed.

sql-chinook-distinct-billing-countries.title: Distinct billing countries
sql-chinook-distinct-billing-countries.prompt_md:
Finance wants the full list of countries the store has ever billed an invoice to. From the **Invoice** table, return the unique set of `BillingCountry` values.

Output exactly one column named `BillingCountry`, with no duplicates. Sort alphabetically (A to Z).
sql-chinook-distinct-billing-countries.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- your column here
FROM Invoice
-- ensure uniqueness and sort
;
hints: DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row set, so selecting only one column gives unique values of that column.
Alphabetical order in SQLite text sorting is the default ascending order.
sql-chinook-distinct-billing-countries.explanation_md: `DISTINCT` collapses repeated `BillingCountry` values to a single row each, and `ORDER BY BillingCountry ASC` returns them in alphabetical order. This is a classic deduplication query.

sql-chinook-customers-in-brazil.title: Customers based in Brazil
sql-chinook-customers-in-brazil.prompt_md:
The support team needs contact details for every customer located in **Brazil**. From the **Customer** table, return the customers whose `Country` is exactly `'Brazil'`.

Output exactly three columns named `FirstName`, `LastName`, and `Email`. Sort by `LastName` ascending, then `FirstName` ascending.
sql-chinook-customers-in-brazil.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- your columns here
FROM Customer
WHERE -- filter to Brazil
ORDER BY -- sort here
;
hints: String comparison in SQLite uses single quotes around the literal: `Country = 'Brazil'`.
Use two sort keys so customers with the same last name are ordered by first name.
sql-chinook-customers-in-brazil.explanation_md: An equality filter on `Country = 'Brazil'` selects the relevant customers, and a two-key `ORDER BY` (last name, then first name) produces a stable, deterministic ordering of the contact list.

sql-chinook-five-longest-tracks.title: Five longest tracks
sql-chinook-five-longest-tracks.prompt_md:
A radio segment needs the five longest songs in the catalog. From the **Track** table, find the five tracks with the largest `Milliseconds` value, and also express each duration in seconds.

Output exactly three columns: `Name`, `Milliseconds`, and `Seconds`, where `Seconds` is `Milliseconds` divided by `1000.0`. Sort by `Milliseconds` descending and return only the top 5 rows.
sql-chinook-five-longest-tracks.starter_code:
SELECT
  Name,
  Milliseconds,
  -- compute Seconds
FROM Track
ORDER BY -- sort
LIMIT 5;
hints: Use `1000.0` rather than `1000` to avoid integer division in SQLite.
Combine `ORDER BY ... DESC` with `LIMIT 5` to take the top five rows.
sql-chinook-five-longest-tracks.explanation_md: Dividing by `1000.0` (a float literal) forces real-number division so `Seconds` keeps its fractional part. Ordering by `Milliseconds DESC` and applying `LIMIT 5` returns the five longest tracks.

sql-chinook-employees-hired-after-2003.title: Employees hired after 2003
sql-chinook-employees-hired-after-2003.prompt_md:
HR is auditing the staff hired from **2004 onward**. The **Employee** table stores `HireDate` as text in the format `'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'`. Return every employee whose `HireDate` falls on or after January 1, 2004.

Output exactly three columns named `FirstName`, `LastName`, and `HireDate`. Sort by `HireDate` ascending (earliest first).
sql-chinook-employees-hired-after-2003.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- your columns here
FROM Employee
WHERE -- filter on HireDate
ORDER BY HireDate ASC;
hints: ISO-formatted date text sorts and compares correctly as plain strings, so `>=` works without date functions.
Compare against `'2004-01-01 00:00:00'` to include everyone hired on or after that instant.
sql-chinook-employees-hired-after-2003.explanation_md: Because `HireDate` is stored as an ISO-8601 text string (`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`), lexicographic comparison against `'2004-01-01 00:00:00'` correctly behaves as a date comparison. Sorting the same column ascending lists the earliest hires first.

sql-chinook-rock-or-jazz-genre-ids.title: Rock or Jazz genres
sql-chinook-rock-or-jazz-genre-ids.prompt_md:
The catalog team wants the genre records for **Rock** and **Jazz**. From the **Genre** table, return the rows whose `Name` is either `'Rock'` or `'Jazz'`.

Output exactly two columns named `GenreId` and `Name`. Sort by `Name` ascending.
sql-chinook-rock-or-jazz-genre-ids.starter_code:
SELECT
  GenreId,
  Name
FROM Genre
WHERE -- match Rock or Jazz
ORDER BY Name ASC;
hints: `Name IN ('Rock', 'Jazz')` is equivalent to two equality checks joined by OR.
Alphabetically, 'Jazz' comes before 'Rock'.
sql-chinook-rock-or-jazz-genre-ids.explanation_md: The `IN` operator checks membership against a list of literals, which is cleaner than chaining `Name = 'Rock' OR Name = 'Jazz'`. Sorting by `Name` ascending puts Jazz before Rock.

sql-chinook-tracks-with-genre-names.title: List tracks with their genre name
sql-chinook-tracks-with-genre-names.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook database, the music catalog stores each track in the `Track` table with a numeric `GenreId`, while the human-readable genre label lives in the `Genre` table. The catalog team wants a quick count of how many tracks fall into each genre.

Write a query that joins `Track` to `Genre` and returns, for every genre that has at least one track, the genre name and the number of tracks in it.

Output exactly two columns named `genre_name` and `track_count`. Sort by `track_count` in descending order; break ties by `genre_name` in ascending (A-Z) order.
sql-chinook-tracks-with-genre-names.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- genre_name, track_count
FROM Genre g
JOIN Track t ON t.GenreId = g.GenreId
-- GROUP BY ...
-- ORDER BY ...;
hints: Join on Track.GenreId = Genre.GenreId, then GROUP BY the genre.
Add genre_name as a tie-breaker in ORDER BY so the row order is unique.
sql-chinook-tracks-with-genre-names.explanation_md: Inner-join `Track` to `Genre` on `GenreId` so each track carries its genre label, then `GROUP BY` the genre and `COUNT` the tracks. An inner join is enough here because every track we care about has a genre; genres with no tracks are intentionally excluded. The ORDER BY with a secondary key on name makes the result deterministic.

sql-chinook-customer-support-rep-name.title: Show each customer's assigned support rep
sql-chinook-customer-support-rep-name.prompt_md:
In Chinook, every customer is assigned a support representative via `Customer.SupportRepId`, which points to `Employee.EmployeeId`. The operations team wants a clean roster mapping each customer to the employee who supports them.

Write a query that joins `Customer` to `Employee` and returns one row per customer with the customer's full name and their support rep's full name.

Output exactly two columns: `customer_name` (the customer's `FirstName` and `LastName` joined by a single space) and `support_rep_name` (the employee's `FirstName` and `LastName` joined by a single space). Sort by `customer_name` in ascending order.
sql-chinook-customer-support-rep-name.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- customer_name, support_rep_name
FROM Customer c
JOIN Employee e ON e.EmployeeId = c.SupportRepId
-- ORDER BY ...;
hints: The join key is Customer.SupportRepId = Employee.EmployeeId.
Use the || operator to concatenate FirstName, a space, and LastName.
sql-chinook-customer-support-rep-name.explanation_md: This is a straightforward foreign-key join from `Customer.SupportRepId` to `Employee.EmployeeId`. Concatenate first and last names with `||` and a literal space to build the display names. Every customer in this dataset has a support rep, so an inner join returns all 59 customers.

sql-northwind-revenue-by-category.title: Total revenue by product category
sql-northwind-revenue-by-category.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, the merchandising team wants to know which product categories drive the most sales. For each category, compute the total net revenue across all order lines, where a line's revenue is `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`.

Tables involved: `"Order Details"`, `Products`, `Categories`.

Return exactly two columns:
- `CategoryName` — the category name
- `TotalRevenue` — the summed line revenue for that category, rounded to 2 decimal places

Sort the result by `TotalRevenue` in descending order.
sql-northwind-revenue-by-category.starter_code:
SELECT
  c.CategoryName,
  -- compute total net revenue here
  ... AS TotalRevenue
FROM "Order Details" od
JOIN Products p ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
JOIN Categories c ON p.CategoryID = c.CategoryID
GROUP BY c.CategoryName
ORDER BY TotalRevenue DESC;
hints: The discount is a fraction (e.g. 0.05 = 5%), so multiply each line by (1 - Discount).
Quote the table name with spaces as "Order Details" in SQLite.
sql-northwind-revenue-by-category.explanation_md: Join order lines to products to recover each product's category, then to the categories table for the readable name. Net line revenue is unit price times quantity times one minus the discount; summing that per category and rounding gives the KPI. Ordering by total revenue descending surfaces the biggest categories first.

sql-northwind-top-10-products-by-units-s.title: Top 10 products by units sold
sql-northwind-top-10-products-by-units-s.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, the inventory team wants the ten best-selling products by total volume (not revenue). For each product, sum the `Quantity` sold across all order lines.

Tables involved: `"Order Details"`, `Products`.

Return exactly two columns:
- `ProductName` — the product name
- `TotalUnitsSold` — the total quantity sold for that product

Sort by `TotalUnitsSold` in descending order; break ties by `ProductName` in ascending (A→Z) order. Return only the top 10 rows.
sql-northwind-top-10-products-by-units-s.starter_code:
SELECT
  p.ProductName,
  SUM(od.Quantity) AS TotalUnitsSold
FROM "Order Details" od
JOIN Products p ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
GROUP BY p.ProductName
ORDER BY TotalUnitsSold DESC, p.ProductName ASC
LIMIT 10;
hints: Aggregate Quantity per product before sorting.
Add a tie-breaker on ProductName so the top-10 cut is unambiguous.
sql-northwind-top-10-products-by-units-s.explanation_md: Volume is measured by raw `Quantity`, so no price or discount math is needed. Group the order lines by product, sum the quantity, then order descending and limit to 10. The secondary sort on product name makes the result deterministic if two products tie on volume.

sql-northwind-freight-summary-by-country.title: Freight cost summary by shipping country
sql-northwind-freight-summary-by-country.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, the logistics team wants a freight summary per destination country. Work only from the `Orders` table (one row per order). For each `ShipCountry`, report how many orders shipped there, the total freight billed, and the average freight per order.

Return exactly four columns:
- `ShipCountry` — the destination country
- `OrderCount` — number of orders shipped to that country
- `TotalFreight` — sum of `Freight` for those orders, rounded to 2 decimal places
- `AvgFreight` — average `Freight` per order, rounded to 2 decimal places

Sort by `TotalFreight` in descending order; break ties by `ShipCountry` in ascending order.
sql-northwind-freight-summary-by-country.starter_code:
SELECT
  ShipCountry,
  COUNT(*) AS OrderCount,
  ROUND(SUM(Freight), 2) AS TotalFreight,
  ROUND(AVG(Freight), 2) AS AvgFreight
FROM Orders
GROUP BY ShipCountry
ORDER BY TotalFreight DESC, ShipCountry ASC;
hints: Everything you need is on the Orders table — no join needed.
COUNT(*) counts orders; pair SUM and AVG of Freight in the same GROUP BY.
sql-northwind-freight-summary-by-country.explanation_md: Freight is stored directly on each order, so no joins are required — just group `Orders` by `ShipCountry`. COUNT gives the order volume, SUM the total freight, and AVG the per-order freight. Sorting by total freight descending highlights the most freight-heavy markets.

sql-northwind-order-customer-employee-ro.title: Order roster with customer and employee names
sql-northwind-order-customer-employee-ro.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, build a roster that pairs every order with the customer who placed it and the employee who handled it. Join `Orders` to `Customers` (on `CustomerID`) and to `Employees` (on `EmployeeID`).

Return exactly these three columns:
- `OrderID` — the order's id
- `CustomerName` — the customer's `CompanyName`
- `EmployeeName` — the employee's first and last name joined by a single space, e.g. `Nancy Davolio`

Return one row per order. Sort the result by `OrderID` ascending.
sql-northwind-order-customer-employee-ro.starter_code:
SELECT
    -- OrderID, CustomerName, EmployeeName
FROM Orders o
-- join Customers and Employees
;
hints: Orders.CustomerID links to Customers.CustomerID and Orders.EmployeeID links to Employees.EmployeeID.
Use the SQLite concatenation operator || to combine FirstName and LastName with a space in between.
sql-northwind-order-customer-employee-ro.explanation_md: Each order references a customer and an employee by foreign key. Two inner joins bring in the related rows, and string concatenation with `||` builds the full employee name. Sorting by `OrderID` makes the output deterministic.

sql-northwind-product-category-supplier-.title: Product catalog with category and supplier
sql-northwind-product-category-supplier-.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, produce a catalog listing for every product together with the category it belongs to and the supplier that provides it. Join `Products` to `Categories` (on `CategoryID`) and to `Suppliers` (on `SupplierID`).

Return exactly these three columns:
- `ProductName` — from `Products`
- `CategoryName` — from `Categories`
- `SupplierName` — the supplier's `CompanyName`

Return one row per product. Sort the result by `ProductName` ascending.
sql-northwind-product-category-supplier-.starter_code:
SELECT
    -- ProductName, CategoryName, SupplierName
FROM Products p
-- join Categories and Suppliers
;
hints: Products.CategoryID joins to Categories.CategoryID; Products.SupplierID joins to Suppliers.SupplierID.
Both Categories and Suppliers exist for every product, so plain INNER JOINs are enough.
sql-northwind-product-category-supplier-.explanation_md: Products store foreign keys to both Categories and Suppliers. Two inner joins resolve those keys into readable names. Aliasing the supplier's CompanyName to SupplierName keeps the output columns clear and distinct from the category name.

sql-northwind-split-contact-first-last-n.title: Split contact names into first and last
sql-northwind-split-contact-first-last-n.prompt_md:
The CRM team stores each customer's contact as a single `ContactName` field (for example, `Maria Anders`) and wants it split into two fields for a mail-merge. In the **Customers** table every `ContactName` contains exactly one space separating a first name from a last name.

From the **Customers** table, return the `CustomerID`, the original `ContactName`, the part before the first space as `FirstName`, and the part after the first space as `LastName`.

Output exactly four columns named `CustomerID`, `ContactName`, `FirstName`, and `LastName`. Sort by `CustomerID` ascending (A to Z).
sql-northwind-split-contact-first-last-n.starter_code:
SELECT
  CustomerID,
  ContactName
  -- derive FirstName and LastName using substr / instr
FROM Customers
ORDER BY CustomerID ASC;
hints: `instr(text, ' ')` gives the position of the first space; subtract 1 to get the length of the first name.
`substr(text, start)` with no length argument returns the rest of the string from `start` to the end.
sql-northwind-split-contact-first-last-n.explanation_md: `instr(ContactName, ' ')` returns the 1-based position of the first space. `substr(ContactName, 1, pos - 1)` takes everything before it for the first name, and `substr(ContactName, pos + 1)` takes everything after it for the last name. Sorting by `CustomerID` makes the output deterministic.

sql-northwind-vowel-companies-uppercased.title: Vowel-initial companies with uppercased country
sql-northwind-vowel-companies-uppercased.prompt_md:
Marketing is building a feature segment for customers whose company name begins with a vowel, and wants the country name shown in upper case for a banner. From the **Customers** table, keep only rows where `CompanyName` starts with one of the letters A, E, I, O, or U (case-insensitive).

Return the `CompanyName` and the `Country` converted to upper case as `CountryUpper`.

Output exactly two columns named `CompanyName` and `CountryUpper`. Sort by `CompanyName` ascending (A to Z).
sql-northwind-vowel-companies-uppercased.starter_code:
SELECT
  CompanyName,
  -- uppercase the country
FROM Customers
-- keep only vowel-initial company names
ORDER BY CompanyName ASC;
hints: Take the first character with `substr(CompanyName, 1, 1)` and uppercase it before comparing.
`UPPER()` works both in the filter and to build the output column.
sql-northwind-vowel-companies-uppercased.explanation_md: `substr(CompanyName, 1, 1)` grabs the first character, and wrapping it in `UPPER(...)` lets a single `IN ('A','E','I','O','U')` test match regardless of original case. `UPPER(Country)` produces the uppercased display column. Sorting by `CompanyName` makes the result deterministic.

sql-northwind-coalesce-region-customer-c.title: Customer counts per region with NULLs labeled
sql-northwind-coalesce-region-customer-c.prompt_md:
A few customers in the **Customers** table have a missing (`NULL`) `Region`. Operations wants a regional headcount where those missing values are grouped under a single readable label `Unknown` instead of disappearing.

Replace any `NULL` `Region` with the literal text `Unknown`, then count how many customers fall into each resulting region label.

Output exactly two columns named `RegionLabel` and `CustomerCount`. Sort by `CustomerCount` descending, then by `RegionLabel` ascending (A to Z) to break ties.
sql-northwind-coalesce-region-customer-c.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- replace NULL Region with 'Unknown'
  COUNT(*) AS CustomerCount
FROM Customers
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY CustomerCount DESC, RegionLabel ASC;
hints: `COALESCE(col, fallback)` returns the first non-NULL value; here the fallback is the literal string `'Unknown'`.
Group by the same COALESCE expression you select so the NULLs are bucketed together.
sql-northwind-coalesce-region-customer-c.explanation_md: `COALESCE(Region, 'Unknown')` returns the region when present and the fallback text otherwise, so the `NULL` rows collapse into one labeled group. Grouping on the same expression and counting gives the per-label headcount, and the two-key sort makes ties deterministic.

sql-northwind-employee-courtesy-display-.title: Build employee display names
sql-northwind-employee-courtesy-display-.prompt_md:
An internal directory needs a single formatted display name for each employee, combining their courtesy title, first name, and last name with single spaces between the parts (for example, `Ms. Nancy Davolio`). From the **Employees** table, concatenate `TitleOfCourtesy`, `FirstName`, and `LastName` in that order, separated by single spaces.

Return the `EmployeeID` and the assembled `DisplayName`.

Output exactly two columns named `EmployeeID` and `DisplayName`. Sort by `EmployeeID` ascending.
sql-northwind-employee-courtesy-display-.starter_code:
SELECT
  EmployeeID,
  -- concatenate TitleOfCourtesy, FirstName, LastName with spaces
FROM Employees
ORDER BY EmployeeID ASC;
hints: In SQLite, `a || b` joins two strings; chain several `||` to combine more than two.
Insert a literal single-space string `' '` between the name parts.
sql-northwind-employee-courtesy-display-.explanation_md: The SQLite `||` operator concatenates strings; inserting literal `' '` between each column produces the spaced display name. Selecting `EmployeeID` alongside and sorting by it yields a stable, deterministic result.

pandas-chinook-track-count-per-genre.title: Track count per genre
pandas-chinook-track-count-per-genre.prompt_md:
Using the chinook `track` and `genre` DataFrames, count how many tracks belong to each genre.

Return a DataFrame with columns `GenreName` (the genre's `Name`) and `TrackCount` (the number of tracks in that genre). Only include genres that have at least one track. Sort by `TrackCount` in descending order, then by `GenreName` in ascending order to break ties.
pandas-chinook-track-count-per-genre.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# track, genre are preloaded DataFrames
result = ...

Use groupby(...).agg with count on TrackId, then sort_values with ascending=[False, True].
pandas-chinook-track-count-per-genre.explanation_md: Inner-join `track` to `genre` on `GenreId` so each track carries its genre name, then group by the genre name and count `TrackId`. An inner join naturally drops genres with no tracks. Finally sort by count descending with the name as a tie-breaker.

pandas-chinook-invoice-count-and-total-p.title: Invoice count and revenue per billing country
pandas-chinook-invoice-count-and-total-p.prompt_md:
Using the chinook `invoice` DataFrame, summarize sales activity per billing country.

Return a DataFrame with columns `BillingCountry`, `InvoiceCount` (number of invoices for that country), and `TotalRevenue` (the sum of the invoice `Total` column, rounded to 2 decimals). Sort by `TotalRevenue` in descending order, then by `BillingCountry` in ascending order to break ties.
pandas-chinook-invoice-count-and-total-p.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# invoice is a preloaded DataFrame
result = ...
hints: A single groupby on BillingCountry can produce both the count and the sum.
Round TotalRevenue after aggregating, then sort_values on it descending.
pandas-chinook-invoice-count-and-total-p.explanation_md: Group the `invoice` DataFrame by `BillingCountry`, then aggregate two metrics in one pass: a count of `InvoiceId` and a sum of `Total`. Round the revenue to 2 decimals and sort by revenue descending with country as the tie-breaker.

pandas-chinook-avg-track-length-by-media.title: Average track length by media type
pandas-chinook-avg-track-length-by-media.prompt_md:
Using the chinook `track` and `media_type` DataFrames, compute the average track length for each media type.

Return a DataFrame with columns `MediaType` (the media type's `Name`) and `AvgMinutes` (the mean of `Milliseconds` converted to minutes, i.e. divided by 60000, rounded to 2 decimals). Sort by `AvgMinutes` in descending order, then by `MediaType` in ascending order to break ties.
pandas-chinook-avg-track-length-by-media.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# track, media_type are preloaded DataFrames
result = ...
hints: Convert Milliseconds to minutes by dividing by 60000 before aggregating.
Group on the media type Name and use mean, then round and sort descending.
pandas-chinook-avg-track-length-by-media.explanation_md: Join `track` to `media_type` on `MediaTypeId` to attach the media type name, derive a minutes column from `Milliseconds` (divide by 60000), then group by the media type name and take the mean. Round to 2 decimals and sort by the average descending.

pandas-chinook-long-tracks-over-five-min.title: Tracks longer than five minutes
pandas-chinook-long-tracks-over-five-min.prompt_md:

LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY sales_year) gives the previous year's revenue; the first row's LAG is NULL.
sql-chinook-yearly-revenue-yoy-change.explanation_md: First aggregate line revenue per year with `strftime('%Y', InvoiceDate)` to extract the year. Then use the `LAG()` window function ordered by year to fetch the prior year's revenue and subtract it. `LAG` returns `NULL` for the first row, which correctly leaves `yoy_change` empty for the earliest year.

sql-chinook-monthly-revenue-2023.title: Monthly revenue for 2023
sql-chinook-monthly-revenue-2023.prompt_md:
The finance team wants a month-by-month revenue breakdown for the year **2023** only, using the Chinook `Invoice` and `InvoiceLine` tables.

For every month of 2023 in which there was at least one invoice, return:
- `year_month` — the month as a `'YYYY-MM'` text string (e.g. `'2023-04'`)
- `revenue` — total line revenue (`InvoiceLine.UnitPrice * InvoiceLine.Quantity`) for that month, rounded to 2 decimals

Sort the result by `year_month` ascending.
sql-chinook-monthly-revenue-2023.starter_code:
-- Filter to 2023, group by calendar month.
SELECT
  -- year_month, revenue
FROM Invoice i
JOIN InvoiceLine il ON il.InvoiceId = i.InvoiceId
WHERE strftime('%Y', i.InvoiceDate) = '2023'
;
hints: strftime('%Y-%m', InvoiceDate) produces a sortable 'YYYY-MM' month label.
Filter the year in the WHERE clause before grouping by month.
sql-chinook-monthly-revenue-2023.explanation_md: Restrict rows to 2023 using `strftime('%Y', InvoiceDate) = '2023'`, then group by the `'YYYY-MM'` month key produced by `strftime('%Y-%m', InvoiceDate)`. Summing `UnitPrice * Quantity` across the joined invoice lines gives monthly revenue.

sql-chinook-acquisition-cohort-by-year.title: Customer acquisition cohorts by first-purchase year
sql-chinook-acquisition-cohort-by-year.prompt_md:
A customer's **acquisition year** is the calendar year of their first-ever invoice. Using the Chinook `Invoice` table, count how many customers were acquired in each year.

Return exactly two columns:
- `cohort_year` — the first-purchase year as an integer
- `customer_count` — the number of customers whose first purchase fell in that year

Sort the result by `cohort_year` ascending.
sql-chinook-acquisition-cohort-by-year.starter_code:
-- Find each customer's first invoice date, then bucket by its year.
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT CustomerId, MIN(date(InvoiceDate)) AS first_date
  FROM Invoice
  GROUP BY CustomerId
)
SELECT
  -- cohort_year, customer_count
FROM firsts
;
hints: MIN(InvoiceDate) per customer gives their first purchase; do this in a CTE first.
Count customers after grouping the first-purchase dates by their year.
sql-chinook-acquisition-cohort-by-year.explanation_md: First reduce each customer to their earliest invoice date with `MIN(date(InvoiceDate))` grouped by `CustomerId`. Then extract the year from that first date with `strftime('%Y', ...)` and count customers per acquisition year. This is a classic cohort sizing query.

sql-chinook-employee-tenure-years.title: Employee tenure in whole years
sql-chinook-employee-tenure-years.prompt_md:
HR needs a tenure report from the Chinook `Employee` table. Treat the reference date as **2025-12-31** and compute each employee's completed years of service since their `HireDate`.

Return exactly four columns:
- `EmployeeId`
- `employee_name` — `FirstName` and `LastName` joined by a single space
- `hire_date` — the hire date as a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` text string (date part only)
- `tenure_years` — completed whole years between `HireDate` and `2025-12-31`, computed as the integer part of `(julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(HireDate)) / 365.25`

Sort by `tenure_years` descending, then by `EmployeeId` ascending.
sql-chinook-employee-tenure-years.starter_code:
-- Compute whole years of service as of 2025-12-31.
SELECT
  -- EmployeeId, employee_name, hire_date, tenure_years
FROM Employee
;
hints: julianday(a) - julianday(b) gives the number of days between two timestamps.
Divide elapsed days by 365.25 and CAST to INTEGER to truncate to whole years.
sql-chinook-employee-tenure-years.explanation_md: `julianday()` converts each timestamp to a fractional day number, so subtracting hire date from the reference date yields elapsed days. Dividing by 365.25 (accounting for leap years) and casting to INTEGER truncates to completed years. `date(HireDate)` strips the time portion for display, and `||` concatenates the name.

sql-chinook-revenue-by-genre.title: Total revenue by genre
sql-chinook-revenue-by-genre.prompt_md:
The Chinook label wants to know which musical genres actually drive sales. Revenue for a sold line item is `InvoiceLine.UnitPrice * InvoiceLine.Quantity`. Each invoice line references a track (`InvoiceLine.TrackId` -> `Track.TrackId`), and each track has a genre (`Track.GenreId` -> `Genre.GenreId`).

Write a query that walks `Genre` -> `Track` -> `InvoiceLine` and computes total revenue per genre. Only include genres that have generated at least one sale.

Output exactly two columns: `genre_name` and `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 decimal places). Sort by `total_revenue` in descending order; break ties by `genre_name` in ascending order.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-genre.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- genre_name, total_revenue
FROM Genre g
JOIN Track t ON t.GenreId = g.GenreId
JOIN InvoiceLine il ON il.TrackId = t.TrackId
-- GROUP BY ...
-- ORDER BY ...;
hints: Join path: Genre -> Track on GenreId, then Track -> InvoiceLine on TrackId.
Revenue per line is UnitPrice * Quantity; SUM it per genre and ROUND to 2 places.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-genre.explanation_md: Chain two inner joins so each invoice line is tagged with its genre, then aggregate `SUM(UnitPrice * Quantity)` per genre. Using inner joins automatically drops genres that never sold (which is the requested behavior). `ROUND(..., 2)` keeps the money values clean and makes grading exact.

sql-chinook-revenue-by-artist-top10.title: Top 10 artists by track sales revenue
sql-chinook-revenue-by-artist-top10.prompt_md:
Chinook wants to reward its best-selling recording artists. The full chain from a sale back to an artist is: `InvoiceLine` -> `Track` (`TrackId`) -> `Album` (`AlbumId`) -> `Artist` (`ArtistId`). Line revenue is `InvoiceLine.UnitPrice * InvoiceLine.Quantity`.

Write a query that joins all four tables and computes total sales revenue per artist, then returns the top 10 artists by revenue.

Output exactly two columns: `artist_name` and `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 decimal places). Sort by `total_revenue` in descending order; break ties by `artist_name` in ascending order. Return only the top 10 rows.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-artist-top10.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- artist_name, total_revenue
FROM Artist ar
JOIN Album al ON al.ArtistId = ar.ArtistId
JOIN Track t ON t.AlbumId = al.AlbumId
JOIN InvoiceLine il ON il.TrackId = t.TrackId
-- GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10;
hints: You need four tables: InvoiceLine, Track, Album, Artist.
Aggregate SUM(UnitPrice*Quantity) per artist, then ORDER BY revenue DESC and LIMIT 10.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-artist-top10.explanation_md: Revenue must be traced through a four-table join because tracks belong to albums and albums belong to artists. After joining `InvoiceLine` -> `Track` -> `Album` -> `Artist`, aggregate revenue per artist and apply `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10`. The name tie-breaker guarantees a single correct ordering even when two artists earn the same amount.

sql-chinook-revenue-by-support-rep.title: Sales revenue attributed to each support rep
sql-chinook-revenue-by-support-rep.prompt_md:
Chinook attributes every customer's purchases to that customer's support representative. The chain is `Employee` -> `Customer` (via `Customer.SupportRepId = Employee.EmployeeId`) -> `Invoice` (via `Invoice.CustomerId = Customer.CustomerId`). Use `Invoice.Total` as the revenue of an invoice.

Write a query that returns, for every employee who is the support rep of at least one customer with at least one invoice, the rep's name, the number of distinct customers they support, and their total attributed revenue.

Output exactly three columns: `support_rep_name` (employee `FirstName` and `LastName` joined by a single space), `customer_count` (count of distinct customers), and `total_revenue` (sum of `Invoice.Total`, rounded to 2 decimal places). Sort by `total_revenue` in descending order; break ties by `support_rep_name` in ascending order.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-support-rep.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- support_rep_name, customer_count, total_revenue
FROM Employee e
JOIN Customer c ON c.SupportRepId = e.EmployeeId
JOIN Invoice i ON i.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
-- GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ...;
hints: Join Employee -> Customer on SupportRepId, then Customer -> Invoice on CustomerId.
Use COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerId) so repeated invoices don't inflate the customer count.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-support-rep.explanation_md: Join `Employee` to `Customer` on the support-rep foreign key, then to `Invoice` on the customer key, so each invoice is attributed to a rep. Use `COUNT(DISTINCT c.CustomerId)` because joining to `Invoice` multiplies customer rows, and `SUM(i.Total)` for revenue. The inner joins naturally restrict the result to the three employees who actually support paying customers.

sql-chinook-customer-distinct-genre-coun.title: How many distinct genres each customer has bought
sql-chinook-customer-distinct-genre-coun.prompt_md:
The marketing team wants to find Chinook's most musically adventurous customers — those who buy across many genres. The path from a customer to a genre is: `Customer` -> `Invoice` (`CustomerId`) -> `InvoiceLine` (`InvoiceId`) -> `Track` (`TrackId`) -> `Genre` (`GenreId`).

Write a query that returns, for each customer who has made at least one purchase, the number of distinct genres they have ever purchased a track from. Return only the top 10 customers by that count.

Output exactly two columns: `customer_name` (customer `FirstName` and `LastName` joined by a single space) and `distinct_genres` (count of distinct genres). Sort by `distinct_genres` in descending order; break ties by `customer_name` in ascending order. Return only the top 10 rows.
sql-chinook-customer-distinct-genre-coun.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- customer_name, distinct_genres
FROM Customer c
JOIN Invoice i ON i.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
JOIN InvoiceLine il ON il.InvoiceId = i.InvoiceId
JOIN Track t ON t.TrackId = il.TrackId
-- GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10;
hints: The genre lives on Track, so join Customer -> Invoice -> InvoiceLine -> Track.
COUNT(DISTINCT Track.GenreId) gives genre breadth per customer.
sql-chinook-customer-distinct-genre-coun.explanation_md: Walk the four-table path from customer down to track, then count distinct `GenreId` per customer with `COUNT(DISTINCT t.GenreId)`. The DISTINCT is essential because a customer typically buys many tracks within the same genre, and we only want each genre counted once. Order by the count and apply LIMIT 10 with a name tie-breaker for determinism.

sql-chinook-revenue-by-customer-country.title: Customer count and revenue by country
sql-chinook-revenue-by-customer-country.prompt_md:
Chinook's finance team wants a per-country sales summary based on where customers are located. Use `Customer.Country` for the country, join `Customer` to `Invoice` on `CustomerId`, and use `Invoice.Total` as the invoice revenue.

Write a query that returns, for each country that has at least one paying customer, the number of distinct customers and the total revenue.

Output exactly three columns: `country`, `customer_count` (distinct customers in that country), and `total_revenue` (sum of `Invoice.Total`, rounded to 2 decimal places). Sort by `total_revenue` in descending order; break ties by `country` in ascending order.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-customer-country.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- country, customer_count, total_revenue
FROM Customer c
JOIN Invoice i ON i.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
-- GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ...;
hints: Group by Customer.Country after joining to Invoice.
Use COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerId) for the customer count and SUM(Total) for revenue.
sql-chinook-revenue-by-customer-country.explanation_md: Join `Customer` to `Invoice` on `CustomerId` so each invoice carries the customer's country, then group by country. Because one customer can have many invoices, `COUNT(DISTINCT c.CustomerId)` is required to count people rather than invoices. The inner join restricts the output to countries that actually generated sales.

sql-chinook-customers-above-average-spen.title: Customers who spend above the average customer
sql-chinook-customers-above-average-spen.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook database (`Customer`, `Invoice`), find every customer whose **total lifetime spend** is strictly greater than the **average total spend across all customers**. Total spend for a customer is the sum of `Invoice.Total` over all of that customer's invoices. The benchmark is the average of those per-customer totals (i.e. average one value per customer, not an average over raw invoices).

Return exactly these columns: `CustomerId`, `FirstName`, `LastName`, `total_spent` (rounded to 2 decimals). Sort by `total_spent` descending, breaking ties by `CustomerId` ascending.

Every customer in this dataset has at least one invoice, so no customer is excluded for lack of orders.
hints: First collapse invoices to a single total per customer in a CTE.
Reference that same CTE in a scalar subquery `(SELECT AVG(total_spent) FROM customer_spend)` for the comparison.
sql-chinook-customers-above-average-spen.explanation_md: Aggregate invoices to one total per customer inside a CTE. Then a scalar subquery computes the average of those per-customer totals, and the outer query keeps only customers above that benchmark. Computing the average from the CTE (one value per customer) — rather than averaging raw invoice rows — is what makes the benchmark correct.

sql-chinook-genres-never-purchased.title: Genres that were never purchased
sql-chinook-genres-never-purchased.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook database (`Genre`, `Track`, `InvoiceLine`), list every genre for which **no track has ever appeared on an invoice line** (i.e. the genre has zero sales). A genre counts as sold if at least one of its tracks shows up in `InvoiceLine`.

Return exactly these columns: `GenreId`, `Name`. Sort by `GenreId` ascending.

Use a correlated `NOT EXISTS` (or an equivalent anti-pattern) rather than relying on outer joins.
hints: A genre is 'sold' if any of its tracks joins to an `InvoiceLine` row.
Negate that with `NOT EXISTS`, correlating the inner `Track.GenreId` to the outer `Genre.GenreId`.
sql-chinook-genres-never-purchased.explanation_md: For each genre, the correlated `NOT EXISTS` subquery probes whether any track of that genre was ever sold (joined `Track` to `InvoiceLine`). Genres for which no such row exists are the ones with zero sales. The correlation on `t.GenreId = g.GenreId` ties the inner probe to the outer genre.

sql-chinook-premium-tracks-never-sold.title: Premium-priced tracks that never sold
sql-chinook-premium-tracks-never-sold.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook database (`Track`, `MediaType`, `InvoiceLine`), find all **premium tracks that were never sold**. A premium track is one with `Track.UnitPrice = 1.99`. A track is 'never sold' if it has no matching row in `InvoiceLine`.

Return exactly these columns: `TrackId`, `track_name` (the track's `Name`), `media_type` (the `MediaType.Name`). Sort by `TrackId` ascending.

Use a correlated `NOT EXISTS` subquery against `InvoiceLine`.
sql-chinook-premium-tracks-never-sold.starter_code:
SELECT t.TrackId, t.Name AS track_name, mt.Name AS media_type
FROM Track t
JOIN MediaType mt ON mt.MediaTypeId = t.MediaTypeId
WHERE t.UnitPrice = 1.99
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    -- a sale of this track
  )
ORDER BY t.TrackId;
hints: Filter on `Track.UnitPrice = 1.99` first.
Add `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM InvoiceLine il WHERE il.TrackId = t.TrackId)` to drop any track that was ever sold.
sql-chinook-premium-tracks-never-sold.explanation_md: Filter tracks down to the premium price point, join to `MediaType` for the readable type name, and use a correlated `NOT EXISTS` against `InvoiceLine` to keep only tracks with zero sales. The price filter and the anti-existence check combine to isolate unsold premium inventory.

sql-chinook-customers-bought-jazz-and-bl.title: Customers who bought both Jazz and Blues
sql-chinook-customers-bought-jazz-and-bl.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook database (`Customer`, `Invoice`, `InvoiceLine`, `Track`, `Genre`), find every customer who has purchased **at least one track from the 'Jazz' genre AND at least one track from the 'Blues' genre** (the two purchases may be on the same or different invoices). A purchase chain is `Customer -> Invoice -> InvoiceLine -> Track -> Genre`.

Return exactly these columns: `CustomerId`, `FirstName`, `LastName`, `Country`. Sort by `CustomerId` ascending.

Use two correlated `EXISTS` subqueries (one per genre) so that both conditions must hold.
sql-chinook-customers-bought-jazz-and-bl.starter_code:
SELECT c.CustomerId, c.FirstName, c.LastName, c.Country
FROM Customer c
WHERE EXISTS ( /* bought a Jazz track */ )
  AND EXISTS ( /* bought a Blues track */ )
ORDER BY c.CustomerId;
hints: Write one `EXISTS` that proves the customer bought a Jazz track, correlated on `CustomerId`.
AND it with a second, identical-shaped `EXISTS` for Blues; both must be true.
sql-chinook-customers-bought-jazz-and-bl.explanation_md: Each `EXISTS` block checks, for the current customer, whether at least one purchased track belongs to the target genre by walking `Invoice -> InvoiceLine -> Track -> Genre`. ANDing the two existence checks enforces set intersection: the customer must have bought both Jazz and Blues. Correlating each subquery on `i.CustomerId = c.CustomerId` scopes the probe to that customer.

sql-chinook-top-3-customers-by-spend-per.title: Top 3 customers by spend in each country
sql-chinook-top-3-customers-by-spend-per.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook tables `Customer`, `Invoice`, and `InvoiceLine`, find the **top 3 highest-spending customers within each country**.

A customer's total spend is the sum of `InvoiceLine.UnitPrice * InvoiceLine.Quantity` across all of their invoice lines (join `Customer` -> `Invoice` -> `InvoiceLine`). Rank customers **within their own `Country`** by total spend, highest first. When two customers in the same country have the same total spend, break the tie by `CustomerName` (A→Z) so each customer gets a distinct rank.

Return exactly these columns:
- `Country` — the customer's country
- `CustomerName` — the customer's first and last name joined by a single space (`FirstName || ' ' || LastName`)
- `TotalSpent` — total spend rounded to 2 decimals
- `SpendRank` — the customer's within-country rank (1 = top spender)

Keep only rows where `SpendRank <= 3`. Sort the result by `Country` ascending, then by `SpendRank` ascending.
sql-chinook-top-3-customers-by-spend-per.starter_code:
-- Compute per-customer spend, rank within each country, keep the top 3
WITH spend AS (
  -- SUM(UnitPrice*Quantity) per customer, grouped by CustomerId
)
SELECT /* Country, CustomerName, TotalSpent, SpendRank */
FROM /* ranked spend */
WHERE SpendRank <= 3
ORDER BY Country ASC, SpendRank ASC;
hints: Aggregate spend per customer first, then rank in a second step — you can't filter on a window function in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
PARTITION BY Country restarts the ranking for every country; add CustomerName as a tiebreaker so ranks are unique.
sql-chinook-top-3-customers-by-spend-per.explanation_md: Aggregate line revenue per customer in a CTE, then use `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Country ORDER BY TotalSpent DESC, CustomerName ASC)` to assign a tie-broken rank inside each country. Filtering the windowed result to `SpendRank <= 3` yields the top-N-per-group. Window functions can't be used directly in `WHERE`, so the ranking lives in a separate CTE/subquery.

sql-chinook-monthly-running-total-revenu.title: Running total of monthly revenue
sql-chinook-monthly-running-total-revenu.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook `Invoice` table, build a month-by-month revenue series with a **cumulative (running) total**.

For each calendar month, sum `Invoice.Total` to get that month's revenue. Then compute a running total that accumulates revenue from the earliest month up to and including the current month.

Return exactly these columns:
- `Month` — the year-month as text in `YYYY-MM` format (use `strftime('%Y-%m', InvoiceDate)`)
- `MonthlyRevenue` — that month's revenue, rounded to 2 decimals
- `RunningTotal` — cumulative revenue through that month, rounded to 2 decimals

Sort the result by `Month` ascending.
hints: Aggregate to one row per month first, then apply the window function over those monthly rows.
An ordered SUM() OVER (...) with frame UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW gives a running total.
sql-chinook-monthly-running-total-revenu.explanation_md: First collapse invoices into one row per `YYYY-MM` month with `strftime` and `SUM(Total)`. Then a cumulative `SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY Month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` adds each month's revenue to everything before it, producing the running total. Because `Month` is a zero-padded `YYYY-MM` string, lexical ordering equals chronological ordering.

sql-chinook-month-over-month-revenue-cha.title: Month-over-month revenue change with LAG
sql-chinook-month-over-month-revenue-cha.prompt_md:
Using the Chinook `Invoice` table, compute **month-over-month revenue change**.

For each calendar month, sum `Invoice.Total` to get monthly revenue. Then, for every month, look up the immediately preceding month's revenue and compute the absolute change.

Return exactly these columns:
- `Month` — year-month as text in `YYYY-MM` format (`strftime('%Y-%m', InvoiceDate)`)
- `MonthlyRevenue` — current month's revenue, rounded to 2 decimals
- `PrevMonthRevenue` — previous month's revenue, rounded to 2 decimals (NULL for the very first month)
- `RevenueChange` — `MonthlyRevenue - PrevMonthRevenue`, rounded to 2 decimals (NULL for the first month)

Include the first month (its `PrevMonthRevenue` and `RevenueChange` will be NULL). Treat the months as a contiguous ordered sequence — "previous month" means the previous row in date order, not a calendar-gap calculation. Sort the result by `Month` ascending.
hints: LAG(col) OVER (ORDER BY Month) returns the value from the previous month's row.
The first month has no predecessor, so LAG yields NULL there — that is expected output.
sql-chinook-month-over-month-revenue-cha.explanation_md: After aggregating revenue per `YYYY-MM` month, `LAG(MonthlyRevenue) OVER (ORDER BY Month)` pulls the prior row's value into the current row. Subtracting it gives the month-over-month delta. `LAG` returns NULL for the first row (no predecessor), which is why the earliest month has NULL change.

sql-northwind-aov-by-employee.title: Average order value by employee
sql-northwind-aov-by-employee.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, sales management wants the top sellers by average order value (AOV). First compute each order's net revenue as the sum of its line revenues `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`. Then, per employee, compute how many orders they handled and their average order revenue.

Tables involved: `Orders`, `"Order Details"`, `Employees`.

Return exactly three columns:
- `EmployeeName` — the employee's first and last name joined by a single space, e.g. `Nancy Davolio`
- `NumOrders` — the number of distinct orders that employee handled
- `AvgOrderValue` — the average per-order net revenue, rounded to 2 decimal places

Sort by `AvgOrderValue` in descending order; break ties by `EmployeeName` ascending. Return only the top 5 rows.
sql-northwind-aov-by-employee.starter_code:
WITH order_rev AS (
  SELECT o.OrderID, o.EmployeeID,
         SUM(od."UnitPrice" * od.Quantity * (1 - od.Discount)) AS OrderRevenue
  FROM Orders o
  JOIN "Order Details" od ON o.OrderID = od.OrderID
  GROUP BY o.OrderID, o.EmployeeID
)
SELECT
  -- employee name, order count, and AOV
  ...
FROM order_rev r
JOIN Employees e ON r.EmployeeID = e.EmployeeID
GROUP BY r.EmployeeID
ORDER BY AvgOrderValue DESC, EmployeeName ASC
LIMIT 5;
hints: Collapse order lines to one revenue figure per order first, then average those.
Use the || operator to build 'First Last' in SQLite.
sql-northwind-aov-by-employee.explanation_md: AOV must be computed at the order grain, so the CTE first rolls line revenue up to one row per order (carrying the EmployeeID). The outer query then averages those order totals per employee — averaging at the order level rather than the line level is the key subtlety. COUNT(*) over the per-order rows yields the order count, and the name is built by concatenating first and last name.

sql-northwind-discount-impact-by-categor.title: Discount impact by category
sql-northwind-discount-impact-by-categor.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, finance wants to quantify how much revenue each category gives away in discounts. For every category compute, across all order lines:
- gross revenue = `SUM("Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity)` (before discount)
- net revenue = `SUM("Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount))` (after discount)
- discount given = `SUM("Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * Discount)`
- the discount given as a percentage of gross revenue

Tables involved: `"Order Details"`, `Products`, `Categories`.

Return exactly five columns:
- `CategoryName`
- `GrossRevenue` — rounded to 2 decimals
- `NetRevenue` — rounded to 2 decimals
- `DiscountGiven` — rounded to 2 decimals
- `DiscountPct` — `100 * DiscountGiven / GrossRevenue`, rounded to 2 decimals

Sort by `DiscountPct` in descending order; break ties by `CategoryName` ascending.
sql-northwind-discount-impact-by-categor.starter_code:
SELECT
  c.CategoryName,
  ROUND(SUM(od."UnitPrice" * od.Quantity), 2) AS GrossRevenue,
  -- net revenue, discount given, and discount percentage
  ...
FROM "Order Details" od
JOIN Products p ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
JOIN Categories c ON p.CategoryID = c.CategoryID
GROUP BY c.CategoryName
ORDER BY DiscountPct DESC, c.CategoryName ASC;
hints: DiscountGiven = UnitPrice * Quantity * Discount, summed per category.
Multiply by 100.0 (not 100) so SQLite does floating-point division.
sql-northwind-discount-impact-by-categor.explanation_md: Gross is price times quantity ignoring discount; the discount given is that same base times the discount fraction; net is gross minus discount. Computing all three as parallel SUMs over the joined order lines keeps them consistent. The discount percentage uses 100.0 (a float) to force real division in SQLite, and sorting by it ranks the most discount-heavy categories first.

sql-northwind-top-product-per-category.title: Best-selling product within each category
sql-northwind-top-product-per-category.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, the category managers each want to know their single best-selling product by net revenue. Net line revenue is `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`. For every category, find the one product with the highest total net revenue.

Tables involved: `"Order Details"`, `Products`, `Categories`.

Return exactly three columns:
- `CategoryName` — the category name
- `ProductName` — the top product in that category
- `Revenue` — that product's total net revenue, rounded to 2 decimals

Within a category, if two products tie on revenue, pick the one whose `ProductName` is alphabetically first. Sort the final result (one row per category) by `Revenue` in descending order.
sql-northwind-top-product-per-category.starter_code:
WITH prod_rev AS (
  SELECT p.CategoryID, p.ProductID, p.ProductName,
         SUM(od."UnitPrice" * od.Quantity * (1 - od.Discount)) AS Revenue
  FROM "Order Details" od
  JOIN Products p ON od.ProductID = p.ProductID
  GROUP BY p.CategoryID, p.ProductID, p.ProductName
)
-- rank products within each category and keep rank 1
SELECT ...
ORDER BY Revenue DESC;
hints: Aggregate revenue per product first, then rank within the category partition.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CategoryID ORDER BY Revenue DESC, ProductName ASC) then filter rn = 1.
sql-northwind-top-product-per-category.explanation_md: This is a classic top-1-per-group problem. First aggregate net revenue per product (keeping its CategoryID). Then ROW_NUMBER, partitioned by category and ordered by revenue descending with a name tie-breaker, ranks products inside each category; keeping rank 1 yields each category's leader. The deterministic tie-break ensures exactly one product per category is returned.

sql-northwind-aov-discounted-vs-fullpric.title: AOV for discounted vs full-price orders
sql-northwind-aov-discounted-vs-fullpric.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, pricing analytics wants to compare average order value (AOV) between orders that contained at least one discounted line and orders that were entirely full price. An order is `Discounted` if any of its order lines has `Discount > 0`; otherwise it is `Full Price`. Each order's net revenue is the sum of its line revenues `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`.

Tables involved: `Orders`, `"Order Details"`.

Return exactly three columns:
- `OrderType` — either the text `Discounted` or `Full Price`
- `NumOrders` — count of orders in that group
- `AvgOrderValue` — average per-order net revenue for the group, rounded to 2 decimals

Sort by `OrderType` in ascending (alphabetical) order, so `Discounted` comes before `Full Price`.
sql-northwind-aov-discounted-vs-fullpric.starter_code:
WITH order_flags AS (
  SELECT o.OrderID,
         MAX(CASE WHEN od.Discount > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS HasDiscount,
         SUM(od."UnitPrice" * od.Quantity * (1 - od.Discount)) AS OrderRevenue
  FROM Orders o
  JOIN "Order Details" od ON o.OrderID = od.OrderID
  GROUP BY o.OrderID
)
SELECT
  -- label the group, count orders, average the revenue
  ...
FROM order_flags
GROUP BY HasDiscount
ORDER BY OrderType ASC;
hints: MAX(CASE WHEN Discount > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) per order flags whether any line was discounted.
Average the per-order revenue, then group by the discount flag.
sql-northwind-aov-discounted-vs-fullpric.explanation_md: The CTE collapses each order to a single row carrying two things: a flag for whether any line was discounted (MAX of a CASE acts as a boolean OR across lines) and the order's total net revenue. The outer query then buckets orders by that flag, counting them and averaging the order-level revenue. Averaging at the order grain — not the line grain — is what makes this a true AOV comparison.

sql-northwind-revenue-by-category-v2.title: Total revenue by product category
sql-northwind-revenue-by-category-v2.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, compute the total sales revenue for each product category. Line-item revenue is `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`. Join `"Order Details"` to `Products` (on `ProductID`) and then to `Categories` (on `CategoryID`), and aggregate by category.

Return exactly these two columns:
- `CategoryName` — from `Categories`
- `TotalRevenue` — the summed line-item revenue for the category, rounded to 2 decimal places

Return one row per category. Sort by `TotalRevenue` descending; if two categories tie, break the tie by `CategoryName` ascending.
sql-northwind-revenue-by-category-v2.starter_code:
SELECT
    -- CategoryName, TotalRevenue
FROM "Order Details" od
-- join Products and Categories, then GROUP BY
;
hints: The category is not on the order line directly — go through Products to reach Categories.
Remember to apply the (1 - Discount) factor inside the SUM before rounding.
sql-northwind-revenue-by-category-v2.explanation_md: Revenue lives on the order-detail lines, but the category lives two joins away (line -> product -> category). After joining, SUM of the discounted line revenue grouped by category gives the answer. ROUND keeps the totals to cents and the tie-breaking sort makes the output deterministic.

sql-northwind-top-3-products-per-categor.title: Top 3 products per category by units sold
sql-northwind-top-3-products-per-categor.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, find the three best-selling products (by total units sold) within each product category. Total units sold for a product is `SUM("Order Details".Quantity)`. Join `"Order Details"` to `Products` (on `ProductID`) and to `Categories` (on `CategoryID`).

Return exactly these three columns:
- `CategoryName` — from `Categories`
- `ProductName` — from `Products`
- `TotalQuantity` — the sum of `Quantity` for that product

Within each category, rank products by `TotalQuantity` descending, breaking ties by `ProductName` ascending, and keep only the top 3 per category. Sort the final result by `CategoryName` ascending, then `TotalQuantity` descending, then `ProductName` ascending.
hints: Aggregate to one row per product first, then apply a window function over the aggregated rows.
PARTITION BY CategoryName restarts the ranking for each category; filter ROW_NUMBER() <= 3.
sql-northwind-top-3-products-per-categor.explanation_md: First aggregate quantity per product (carrying its category along via two joins). Then use ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by category and ordered by quantity to rank products inside each category, and filter to ranks 1-3. The deterministic tie-break on ProductName guarantees a single correct result set.

sql-northwind-employee-orders-and-revenu.title: Orders handled and revenue per employee
sql-northwind-employee-orders-and-revenu.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, summarize each employee's sales performance: how many distinct orders they handled and the total revenue across those orders. Revenue per line is `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`. Join `Employees` to `Orders` (on `EmployeeID`) and `Orders` to `"Order Details"` (on `OrderID`).

Return exactly these three columns:
- `EmployeeName` — the employee's first and last name joined by a single space
- `OrderCount` — the number of distinct orders the employee handled
- `TotalRevenue` — the summed line-item revenue across those orders, rounded to 2 decimal places

Return one row per employee. Sort by `TotalRevenue` descending; break ties by `EmployeeName` ascending.
sql-northwind-employee-orders-and-revenu.starter_code:
SELECT
    -- EmployeeName, OrderCount, TotalRevenue
FROM Employees e
-- join Orders and "Order Details", then GROUP BY employee
;
hints: Joining to "Order Details" duplicates each order once per line — count distinct OrderIDs, not raw rows.
Group by the employee's primary key so revenue and order count line up per employee.
sql-northwind-employee-orders-and-revenu.explanation_md: Because each order has multiple detail lines, joining all the way to "Order Details" multiplies the order rows, so the order count must use COUNT(DISTINCT o.OrderID). Revenue is the SUM of discounted line revenue. Grouping by the employee key collapses everything to one row per employee.

sql-northwind-top-category-per-shipper.title: Each shipper's highest-revenue category
sql-northwind-top-category-per-shipper.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, for each shipper find the single product category that generated the most revenue on the orders that shipper delivered. `Orders.ShipVia` links to `Shippers.ShipperID`. Line revenue is `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`. You will need to join `Orders` -> `Shippers`, `Orders` -> `"Order Details"` -> `Products` -> `Categories`.

Return exactly these three columns:
- `ShipperName` — the shipper's `CompanyName`
- `TopCategoryName` — the `CategoryName` with the highest revenue shipped by that shipper
- `CategoryRevenue` — that category's revenue via that shipper, rounded to 2 decimal places

Return one row per shipper (the top category only). Within a shipper, rank categories by revenue descending, breaking ties by `CategoryName` ascending. Sort the final result by `ShipperName` ascending.
hints: Orders.ShipVia is the foreign key to Shippers.ShipperID.
Aggregate revenue per shipper-and-category first, then use ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by shipper to keep the top one.
sql-northwind-top-category-per-shipper.explanation_md: This is a five-table chain: orders connect to shippers on one side and reach categories through order lines and products on the other. After aggregating revenue per (shipper, category), ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by shipper and ordered by revenue picks the leading category per shipper. Filtering to rn = 1 yields one row per shipper.

sql-northwind-top-3-customers-by-spend-p.title: Top 3 customers by spend in each country
sql-northwind-top-3-customers-by-spend-p.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database, find the three highest-spending customers in each country. A customer's spend is the sum of `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)` across all of their orders. Join `Customers` -> `Orders` (on `CustomerID`) -> `"Order Details"` (on `OrderID`). Exclude customers whose `Country` is NULL.

Return exactly these three columns:
- `Country` — the customer's country
- `CompanyName` — the customer's company name
- `TotalSpend` — that customer's total spend, rounded to 2 decimal places

Within each country, rank customers by spend descending, breaking ties by `CompanyName` ascending, and keep the top 3 per country. Sort the final result by `Country` ascending, then `TotalSpend` descending, then `CompanyName` ascending.
hints: Group by the customer key so each customer becomes a single row before ranking.
PARTITION BY Country in the window function restarts the ranking per country; keep ROW_NUMBER() <= 3.
sql-northwind-top-3-customers-by-spend-p.explanation_md: Aggregate spend per customer (grouping by the customer key so each customer is one row, carrying country and name). Then ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by country ranks customers within their country, and the filter keeps the top three. Excluding NULL countries and breaking ties on CompanyName keeps the result deterministic.

sql-northwind-contact-title-case-buckets.title: Bucket customer contacts by job family
sql-northwind-contact-title-case-buckets.prompt_md:
Job titles in the **Customers** `ContactTitle` field are inconsistent (for example, `Sales Representative`, `Sales Manager`, `Marketing Assistant`, `Owner/Marketing Assistant`). Sales ops wants them rolled up into broad job families and counted.

Classify each customer's `ContactTitle` with a `CASE` expression, checking the conditions in this exact priority order and stopping at the first match:
1. If it contains `Sales`, label it `Sales`.
2. Otherwise, if it contains `Marketing`, label it `Marketing`.
3. Otherwise, if it contains `Account`, label it `Accounting`.
4. Otherwise, if it contains `Owner`, label it `Ownership`.
5. Otherwise, label it `Other`.

The substring matches are case-sensitive and use the standard `LIKE '%...%'` form. Then count the customers in each label.

Output exactly two columns named `TitleGroup` and `CustomerCount`. Sort by `CustomerCount` descending, then by `TitleGroup` ascending (A to Z) to break ties.
sql-northwind-contact-title-case-buckets.starter_code:
SELECT
  CASE
    -- check Sales, then Marketing, then Account, then Owner, else Other
  END AS TitleGroup,
  COUNT(*) AS CustomerCount
FROM Customers
GROUP BY TitleGroup
ORDER BY CustomerCount DESC, TitleGroup ASC;
hints: `CASE` stops at the first `WHEN` that is true, so branch order matters for titles that contain more than one keyword.
Use `LIKE '%keyword%'` for the substring tests and a trailing `ELSE 'Other'`.
sql-northwind-contact-title-case-buckets.explanation_md: A `CASE` expression evaluates its `WHEN` branches top to bottom and returns the first match, so the listed priority order resolves ambiguous titles like `Owner/Marketing Assistant` (which matches `Marketing` before `Owner`). Grouping by the resulting label and counting produces the per-family totals; the two-key sort breaks count ties alphabetically.

sql-northwind-supplier-fax-fallback-flag.title: Supplier fax fallback and availability flag
sql-northwind-supplier-fax-fallback-flag.prompt_md:
Procurement is exporting a supplier contact sheet from the **Suppliers** table. Many suppliers have a `NULL` `Fax`, which must be displayed as the literal text `N/A`, and the sheet also needs a simple yes/no flag for whether a real fax exists.

For every supplier, return the `CompanyName`, the fax value with `NULL` replaced by `N/A` as `FaxValue`, and a flag `HasFax` that is `Yes` when `Fax` is not `NULL` and `No` when it is `NULL`.

Output exactly three columns named `CompanyName`, `FaxValue`, and `HasFax`. Sort by `CompanyName` ascending (A to Z).
sql-northwind-supplier-fax-fallback-flag.starter_code:
SELECT
  CompanyName,
  -- COALESCE the fax to 'N/A'
  -- CASE flag for HasFax
FROM Suppliers
ORDER BY CompanyName ASC;
hints: Use `COALESCE(Fax, 'N/A')` for the display value and a `CASE` with `IS NULL` for the flag.
You cannot compare to NULL with `=`; always use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`.
sql-northwind-supplier-fax-fallback-flag.explanation_md: `COALESCE(Fax, 'N/A')` substitutes the placeholder text only when the fax is missing. A separate `CASE WHEN Fax IS NULL` builds the explicit `Yes`/`No` availability flag (note that `NULL` must be tested with `IS NULL`, not `=`). Sorting by `CompanyName` makes the export deterministic.

sql-northwind-normalize-customer-phone-d.title: Normalize customer phone numbers to digits
sql-northwind-normalize-customer-phone-d.prompt_md:
Phone numbers in the **Customers** table are stored in many inconsistent formats, such as `(171) 555-7788`, `030-0074321`, and `88.60.15.31`. A data pipeline needs a normalized version containing only the digits, with all formatting characters stripped out.

From `Phone`, remove every occurrence of the following five characters: an opening parenthesis `(`, a closing parenthesis `)`, a hyphen `-`, a space ` `, and a period `.`. Return the `CustomerID`, the original `Phone`, and the cleaned digits-only string as `PhoneDigits`.

Output exactly three columns named `CustomerID`, `Phone`, and `PhoneDigits`. Sort by `CustomerID` ascending (A to Z).
sql-northwind-normalize-customer-phone-d.starter_code:
SELECT
  CustomerID,
  Phone,
  -- strip ( ) - space and . from Phone using nested replace()
FROM Customers
ORDER BY CustomerID ASC;
hints: `replace(s, x, '')` removes all copies of `x`; nest the calls to remove several different characters.
Strip one character per replace: `(`, `)`, `-`, space, and `.`.
sql-northwind-normalize-customer-phone-d.explanation_md: `replace(text, target, '')` deletes every occurrence of `target`. Nesting five `replace` calls strips each unwanted formatting character in turn, leaving only the digits. The original `Phone` is kept alongside for comparison, and sorting by `CustomerID` makes the result deterministic.

sql-northwind-packaging-type-from-quanti.title: Classify products by packaging keyword
sql-northwind-packaging-type-from-quanti.prompt_md:
The **Products** table describes packaging as free text in `QuantityPerUnit`, for example `24 - 12 oz bottles`, `36 boxes`, `12 - 8 oz jars`, `18 - 500 g pkgs.`, and `10 boxes x 20 bags`. Merchandising wants products grouped into packaging types based on a keyword found anywhere in that text.

Classify each product with a `CASE` expression, checking conditions in this exact priority order and stopping at the first match:
1. If `QuantityPerUnit` contains `bottle`, label it `Bottles`.
2. Otherwise, if it contains `box`, label it `Boxes`.
3. Otherwise, if it contains `jar`, label it `Jars`.
4. Otherwise, if it contains `pkg`, label it `Packages`.
5. Otherwise, if it contains `bag`, label it `Bags`.
6. Otherwise, label it `Other`.

Use case-sensitive `LIKE '%...%'` substring matches. Count the products in each packaging type.

Output exactly two columns named `PackagingType` and `ProductCount`. Sort by `ProductCount` descending, then by `PackagingType` ascending (A to Z) to break ties.
sql-northwind-packaging-type-from-quanti.starter_code:
SELECT
  CASE
    -- bottle, then box, then jar, then pkg, then bag, else Other
  END AS PackagingType,
  COUNT(*) AS ProductCount
FROM Products
GROUP BY PackagingType
ORDER BY ProductCount DESC, PackagingType ASC;
hints: `LIKE '%word%'` is true when `word` appears anywhere in the string.
Branch order in `CASE` decides the label for rows whose text contains two keywords.
sql-northwind-packaging-type-from-quanti.explanation_md: Each `CASE` branch tests for a packaging keyword with `LIKE '%keyword%'`, and because `CASE` returns the first matching branch, the listed priority resolves descriptions that mention more than one container (such as `10 boxes x 20 bags`, which matches `box` before `bag`). Grouping by the label and counting gives the per-type totals, with the two-key sort breaking count ties alphabetically.

sql-northwind-products-above-overall-ave.title: Products priced above the overall average
sql-northwind-products-above-overall-ave.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind `Products` table, find every product whose `UnitPrice` is strictly greater than the average `UnitPrice` across all products.

Return exactly these columns:
- `ProductName`
- `UnitPrice`

Sort by `UnitPrice` descending, then by `ProductName` ascending to break ties.
sql-northwind-products-above-overall-ave.starter_code:
SELECT ProductName, UnitPrice
FROM Products
-- compare against the overall average UnitPrice
;
hints: A scalar subquery in the WHERE clause can return the overall average.
Use strictly greater-than so products exactly at the average are excluded.
sql-northwind-products-above-overall-ave.explanation_md: A scalar subquery `(SELECT AVG(UnitPrice) FROM Products)` computes the single overall average, which the outer query compares each row against. Because the subquery is uncorrelated it is evaluated once. The strict `>` excludes products exactly at the average.

sql-northwind-repeat-buyers-order-counts.title: Repeat buyers and their order counts
sql-northwind-repeat-buyers-order-counts.prompt_md:
A 'repeat buyer' is a customer who has placed more than one order. Using the Northwind `Customers` and `Orders` tables, list all repeat buyers along with how many orders each has placed.

Return exactly these columns:
- `CustomerID`
- `CompanyName`
- `OrderCount` (the number of orders for that customer)

Sort by `OrderCount` descending, then by `CustomerID` ascending to break ties.
sql-northwind-repeat-buyers-order-counts.starter_code:
WITH order_counts AS (
  SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount
  FROM Orders
  GROUP BY CustomerID
)
-- keep only customers with more than one order, then join to names
;
hints: GROUP BY CustomerID and filter with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
Join the aggregated counts back to Customers for the company name.
sql-northwind-repeat-buyers-order-counts.explanation_md: A CTE aggregates orders per customer and the `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` filter keeps only those who ordered more than once. The CTE is then joined back to `Customers` to attach company names. Aggregating first keeps the logic readable and the join small.

sql-northwind-products-above-category-av.title: Products priced above their own category average
sql-northwind-products-above-category-av.prompt_md:
For each product, compare its `UnitPrice` against the average `UnitPrice` of all products in the SAME category. Using the Northwind `Products` and `Categories` tables, return every product whose price is strictly greater than its own category's average price.

Return exactly these columns:
- `CategoryName`
- `ProductName`
- `UnitPrice`
- `CategoryAvgPrice` (the average UnitPrice of the product's category, rounded to 2 decimals)

Sort by `CategoryName` ascending, then `UnitPrice` descending, then `ProductName` ascending.
sql-northwind-products-above-category-av.starter_code:
SELECT cat.CategoryName, p.ProductName, p.UnitPrice
FROM Products p
JOIN Categories cat ON cat.CategoryID = p.CategoryID
-- keep products priced above their category's average
;
hints: Compute the per-category average in a CTE grouped by CategoryID.
Join that average back to each product and compare with strict greater-than.
sql-northwind-products-above-category-av.explanation_md: A CTE computes each category's average unit price, then the main query joins it back so every product can be compared to its own category's average. Filtering on `p.UnitPrice > ca.avg_price` keeps the above-average products, and the rounded average is exposed for context. An equivalent correlated subquery per category would also work but the CTE evaluates the averages once.

sql-northwind-top-product-per-category-r.title: Top product per category by revenue
sql-northwind-top-product-per-category-r.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database (tables `Categories`, `Products`, and `"Order Details"`), find the single best-selling product in each product category by total revenue.

Line revenue is `"Order Details".UnitPrice * Quantity * (1 - Discount)`. For every category, identify the product whose total revenue (summed across all order lines) is the highest. If two products in the same category tie on revenue, pick the one whose `ProductName` sorts first alphabetically (A to Z).

Return exactly these three columns, in this order:
- `CategoryName`
- `ProductName`
- `Revenue` — total revenue for that product, rounded to 2 decimal places

Return exactly one row per category. Sort the result by `Revenue` in descending order.
sql-northwind-top-product-per-category-r.starter_code:
SELECT
  -- one row per category: its top product by revenue
FROM "Order Details" od
JOIN Products p ON p.ProductID = od.ProductID
JOIN Categories c ON c.CategoryID = p.CategoryID

;

ROW_NUMBER() with PARTITION BY CategoryName plus a ProductName tie-breaker guarantees exactly one row per category.
sql-northwind-top-product-per-category-r.explanation_md: Aggregate line revenue per product in a CTE, then use `ROW_NUMBER()` partitioned by category and ordered by revenue (descending), with `ProductName` as the tie-breaker. Keeping only `rn = 1` yields the single top product per category. Rounding is applied after aggregation, and the final result is ordered by revenue.

sql-northwind-top-3-products-per-categor.title: Top 3 products per category by units sold
sql-northwind-top-3-products-per-categor.prompt_md:
Using the Northwind database (`Categories`, `Products`, `"Order Details"`), list the top 3 products in each category by total units sold (the sum of `Quantity` across all order lines).

Use `DENSE_RANK()` to rank products within each category by total quantity, highest first, so that products tied on quantity share the same rank. Keep every product whose dense rank is 3 or less (ties at the cutoff are all included).

Return exactly these four columns, in this order:
- `CategoryName`
- `ProductName`
- `TotalQuantity` — total units sold for that product
- `Rnk` — the dense rank within the category (1 = most units)

Sort the result by `CategoryName` ascending, then `Rnk` ascending, then `ProductName` ascending.
